pages.notes: Welcome. This is the year in numbers: what we built, what we repaired, what it cost and what is next. About twenty minutes.

sentence you

pages.notes: Three rules, two examples, one question. People like knowing where the end is.

pages.notes: Rule one. The giant numeral is the point: one. Ask the room to name the last sign they read all of.

Visitors please note that the main lifts to wards 4 to 9 are located beyond the cafe, past reception, on the left after the double doors.
The cafe is still there. Nobody was ever looking for it.
Fourteen fewer people a week asked reception for directions.

pages.notes: Same corridor, same lifts. The old sign tried to be a map. The new one is a signpost. Let the left sign be painfully unreadable from the back of the room.

pages.notes: Arne painted signs for forty years and taught me this at a kitchen table. He would have hated this slide for being a poster.

Put it where
the eyes

People look at doors, at floors and at the person ahead. They do not look up. Mount signs at the height of a handle, or paint them on what everybody walks across.
We moved the pharmacy sign from the ceiling to the floor. It was found 40 seconds sooner, on average.

pages.notes: Rule two is about placement. Ask who looked at the ceiling today.

Not a colleague. Not a client. Stop a stranger at the door, give them four seconds and ask where they were going.

pages.notes: Rule three. Do the test with a stranger, not a friend. Friends know where the lifts are.

Eight months a year nobody is home. The roof is steep, the windows small on the north side and every door can be shut from outside in a storm.

elements.text:
The brief:
a house that survives eight months of nobody home.
Skärgårdshus, Sandhamn. Wind from three sides, salt in everything, one ferry a day in winter.
A family of five wanted it open from May to September and shut and safe from October to April.

pages.notes: Now one project in depth. The brief was the most honest part: a house mostly empty.
